Updated Tue, October 20, 2026 at 5:59 PM UTC
COLUMBUS, Ohio--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct 20, 2026--
Accenture (NYSE: ACN), Dragos Inc. and the SANS Institute today announced a major initiative to help strengthen cyber defenses for under-resourced U.S. water, electric and natural gas utilities. These utilities provide essential services but often lack resources for adequate protection for their operational technology (OT) environments. The announcement comes amid a recent surge in cyberattacks targeting more than 100 U.S. water systems across over a dozen states.
This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261020093364/en/
Accenture, Dragos Inc. and the SANS Institute today announced a major initiative to help strengthen cyber defenses for under-resourced U.S. water, electric and natural gas utilities.
In its first phase, the initiative will provide cybersecurity software, hardware, deployment services and SANS training free of charge to up to 500 under-resourced utilities. Accenture, Dragos and SANS are making an initial combined commitment of approximately $10 million in funding and services. In addition, Elastic is supporting the initiative through technology that allows for software delivery at scale by providing the primary log storage and query engine within the Dragos Platform.
Many of the tens of thousands of small utilities across the U.S., particularly those serving rural or underserved communities, face limited funding, workforce shortages and aging technology. This leaves the pumps, valves, substations and distribution networks that support essential services vulnerable to cyberattacks that can threaten public safety.
To address this gap, Accenture, Dragos and SANS are launching the Community Cyber Resilience Foundation to provide eligible utilities with OT cybersecurity technology, deployment support, hardware and training. The initiative builds on the Dragos Community Defense Program, which provides more than 100 utilities with free access to the Dragos Platform. The foundation was announced at a roundtable discussion focused on strengthening the cybersecurity of utilities in Ohio, hosted by American Electric Power (AEP) subsidiary Ohio Power Company, Accenture and Dragos.
“Our work with America’s critical infrastructure operators has shown both the gravity of the cyber threats they face and a widening vulnerability gap—between large operators with the resources to invest in cybersecurity and smaller utilities that often lack those means,” said Julie Sweet, chair and CEO, Accenture. “Together with Dragos and SANS, we will provide under-resourced utilities with the technology, expertise and training they need to better power and protect the communities they serve.”
“Adversaries are aggressively targeting utilities, attacking the operational environments that provide life-sustaining services to millions of Americans. Yet many small operators lack the capacity to defend against these threats,” said Robert M. Lee, Chairman, CEO, and Founder of Dragos. “The Community Cyber Resilience Foundation gives the utilities that need it most access to cybersecurity resources and training at no cost.”
Who qualifies, how to apply Eligible participants include U.S. based water, wastewater, electric and natural gas utilities with less than $100 million in annual revenue. More than 97% of utilities fall below this threshold, representing more than 50,000 organizations that may need support. Participants can expect:
Access to the Dragos Platform and services to help organizations know what’s on their networks and how to address vulnerabilities and threats. Elasticsearch provides the underlying log storage and search capabilities that help Dragos deliver the platform at scale to participating utilities.
Accenture deployment services including expert configuration, integration and ongoing support.
SANS ICS/OT training to build and sustain in-house capabilities.
Hardware and infrastructurefunding to purchase the equipment needed to deploy and run the Dragos Platform.
Peer community access connecting participants to a network of utilities sharing operational experience.
“ The best security technology in the world won’t protect a utility if its staff are not able to use it. The foundation puts training and skills in the hands of the people protecting the water, power, natural gas, and wastewater treatment systems that communities rely on,” said James Lyne, CEO, SANS.
“Strong cybersecurity depends on many technologies working together. Elastic is committed to supporting Dragos in delivering its platform at scale, helping make advanced cybersecurity capabilities accessible to utilities that could not otherwise afford them,” said Ashutosh Kulkarni, CEO, Elastic.
Utilities interested in participating can learn more at https://www.ccrfoundation.org/.
About the Community Cyber Resilience Foundation The Community Cyber Resilience Foundation is a nonprofit launched by Accenture, Dragos, and the SANS Institute. It raises and provides the funding, hardware, deployment services, and training that small, under-resourced utilities in the U.S. need to secure their operational technology environments. Visit https://www.ccrfoundation.org/.

Our ambition is to be the reinvention partner of choice for our clients and lead in the safe, widespread adoption of AI, and to be the most client-focused, AI-enabled, great place to work in the world. Our approximately 814,000 people bring deep insights across industries and functions, with capabilities spanning strategy, process, operating model, change management, talent, data, technology and AI. We deliver this expertise through consulting, managed services, proprietary assets and platforms, and increasingly, software. The Dragos Platform delivers asset visibility, continuous monitoring, OT vulnerability management, segmentation validation, device protection, and real-time threat detection, powered by the industry’s most experienced OT threat intelligence and incident response team. Dragos serves critical sectors such as energy, manufacturing, water, transportation, data centers, mining, and ports. Privately held and headquartered in the Washington, DC area, Dragos operates globally across North America, EMEA, and APAC. Visit dragos.com.

Today, SANS is the most trusted and, by far, the largest provider of cybersecurity training and certification to professionals in government and commercial institutions worldwide. Renowned SANS instructors teach more than 85 courses at in-person and virtual cybersecurity events and OnDemand. GIAC, an affiliate of the SANS Institute, validates practitioner skills through more than 50 hands-on technical certifications in cybersecurity.

pages.title: Accenture reportedly looks to sell its China business for up to $1.5B
pages.text:
Accenture sign above an entrance in Zurich, Switzerland, in November 2022
Credit: Tobias Arhelger via Shutterstock
Accenture is exploring a sale of its Greater China business, in a deal that could value the unit at up to $1.5bn, the Financial Times reported on Sunday.
The consulting firm has hired JPMorgan to run a strategic review of the unit, according to the Financial Times report, which cited people familiar with the matter. The review follows unsolicited interest in the business over the past year, the paper said.
Accenture and JPMorgan did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Reuters, which were sent outside regular business hours.
The Greater China unit covers mainland China, Hong Kong, and Taiwan, according to Accenture’s website. Its wider Asia-Pacific business brought in about $10bn in revenue last year, the FT said.
A sale would probably draw private equity groups and a small number of strategic buyers, the FT reported. Accenture could also keep a significant minority stake to give clients continuity. However, there is no certainty that the review will lead to a deal.
The FT also pointed to wider pressure on Western advisers in China. Several, including McKinsey, have scaled back there. At the same time, tighter Chinese security rules limit how much sensitive data can leave the country.
Accenture has already signalled that it is willing to sell parts of the company. At a recent investor event, chief financial officer Angie Park said it can raise money by selling assets, according to the FT.
The firm has a record of “exiting businesses, offerings, countries, contracts that no longer meet our strategic or return thresholds,” Park said, according to the FT.
The report comes as Accenture tries to convince investors that AI will bring it more work, not less. Some investors fear AI could let clients bring work in-house, the FT said. In June, its shares suffered their worst one-day drop on record after a weak forecast.
The stock then rose by about a fifth on October 1, after fourth-quarter results beat expectations. Revenue for the year to August rose 6.5% to $74.2bn. For fiscal 2027, the company expects growth of 3% to 6%.
At its investor day on October 14, Accenture said it plans about $8bn of acquisitions in fiscal 2027. That figure includes its deal for industrial security firm Dragos. It also aims to return at least $9.5bn to shareholders next year.
Money from a China sale could help pay for those plans, the FT said.

Accenture Just Capped Employees’ Claude Spending at $29 a Month. Some Were Spending $1,000
Accenture sells AI transformation to thousands of clients while quietly telling its own employees they get a fraction of what some were already spending. The internal memo reveals a tension at the heart of every major consulting firm racing to…
Published October 16, 2026, 9:27am ET · 3 min read
A businessman engages in strategic planning amidst a backdrop of global AI innovation and financial data. The image underscores the intricate balance between technological advancement and sound personal finance in the rapidly evolving digital landscape. © MUNGKHOOD STUDIO / Shutterstock.com
An Accenture (NYSE:ACN | ACN Price Prediction) consultant building an AI solution for several clients said Claude Code usage ran between $500 and $1,000 a month. Starting October 1, the company will centrally fund $29 per person.
Accenture told many employees in an internal memo, reported on October 15, 2026, that it will pay only that fixed monthly amount toward Claude, the AI model built by privately held Anthropic. Anything above it must be charged to a project.
Accenture sells AI transformation to roughly 9,000 clients. Internally, it now limits spending on the same tools.
Shares rose 4.63% to $224.92 on October 15 during a broad software rally unrelated to the memo, yet they remain well below the 52-week high of $291.09.
What Accenture’s Claude Memo Actually Commits To
The memo, titled “Claude Enterprise Users: Important Updates to Licensing and Usage Costs,” states that “all costs are consumption-based.” Usage above the allowance goes to a Work Breakdown Structure (WBS), Accenture’s billing code for a project or team.
Heavy use remains possible, but it now needs a budget owner. Premium plans include $250 of weekly token usage, although many employees are not on Premium.
Access is conditional. The memo says, “Providing a WBS and obtaining a license does not guarantee indefinite or ongoing access to Claude,” and one employee lost access entirely.
Accenture did not publish the memo or say how many employees are affected. A spokesperson said, “Our approach today is to provide the right tool for the right work.”
Consumption Billing Shows What Coding AI Really Costs
The $29 cap targets a consumer subscription price point. Agentic coding tools, which carry out complex tasks on their own, consume far more tokens, the units AI models bill by.
One employee said usage topped $500 a month for months, and some spent as much as $1,000. Per-seat budgets are likely to fall short once work shifts to autonomous coding.
CEO Julie Sweet said on the October 1 earnings call that falling token costs will “enable companies to use AI in more places and at scale.” The memo suggests that prices likely have further to fall before agentic coding becomes cheap enough to fund on a per-seat basis.
Accenture earns its margin on labor across roughly 814,000 employees. Unlimited token spending on that base is a cost that grows without a matching revenue line.
Charging overruns to a WBS ties AI spending to client work. Fixed-price work is over 65% of bookings, so AI costs on those contracts land on Accenture unless they were priced in.
Management guided to a 15.9% to 16.1% operating margin for fiscal 2027, which leaves little room for unmanaged expense.

Accenture plc acquired Miami-based Avicado to expand its digital construction services for major capital projects. Accenture (ACN) stock climbed 0.72% to $238.63, gaining $1.70 after reversing earlier losses. The acquisition strengthens Accenture Construct’s software integration and project management services across complex infrastructure developments.
Accenture Expands Digital Construction Consulting Capabilities
Accenture Construct will absorb Avicado’s consulting operations, widening its support for infrastructure owners and developers. The acquisition adds expertise in connecting construction software, improving project controls, and organizing complex workflows. As a result, project owners can manage data more efficiently and reduce manual handoffs between teams.
Avicado began operations in 2015 and maintains its headquarters in Miami, Florida. The consultancy helps organizations connect construction platforms and improve reporting throughout major projects. Its approach combines technology implementation with operational support for clients managing complex construction programs.
More than 190 Avicado employees will join Accenture Construct’s United States team. Their experience strengthens the unit’s ability to manage digital systems and construction delivery requirements. Accenture plans to combine these capabilities with its existing industry expertise and artificial intelligence services.
Avicado Brings Construction Software and Project Management Expertise
Avicado works with major construction software providers, including Procore, Autodesk, Trimble, Oracle and Kahua. The firm implements Autodesk Construction Cloud, BIM 360, Oracle Primavera P6, and Textura. Its specialists also support Trimble’s e-Builder platform and integrate software across project workflows.
Beyond software implementation, Avicado assists project owners with planning and daily program delivery. Its specialists handle feasibility reviews, site selection, procurement, scheduling, and document management. They act as owner representatives and help oversee work across multiple project teams.
Avicado serves data center operators, transportation agencies, government bodies, and commercial property developers. Its customers also span education, healthcare, manufacturing, energy, water, and wastewater sectors. These industries require extensive planning, project controls, and reliable records throughout construction.
Accenture Strengthens Infrastructure Services Through Avicado Acquisition
The acquisition expands Accenture Construct’s ability to support complex capital programs across several industries. By adding Avicado’s specialists, Accenture gains deeper expertise in construction platforms and project delivery. The combination also supports its strategy of connecting technology, operational processes, and project management services.
The deal strengthens Accenture’s position in digital consulting for infrastructure development. Avicado’s experience with major construction platforms complements Accenture’s broader technology and systems integration capabilities. These services can help project owners improve coordination, manage information, and strengthen operational oversight.
Accenture did not disclose the acquisition price or provide specific financial projections for the transaction. Consequently, the deal’s direct contribution to revenue and earnings remains unclear. Nevertheless, the acquisition broadens Accenture’s construction consulting capabilities and extends its reach across capital-intensive industries.

Accenture (NYSE: ACN) has acquired Avicado, a construction technology consultancy headquartered in Miami. Digital-native construction consulting firm Avicado joins Accenture Construct to expand digital and systems consulting capabilities for capital projects owners.
Founded in 2015, Avicado helps clients improve project delivery through connected systems, stronger project controls and better use of data. The digital-native company specializes in implementing and integrating leading construction and project management software from Procore, Autodesk (Construction Cloud, BIM 360), Trimble (Trimble Unity construct/e-builder), Oracle (Primavera P6, Textura) and Kahua.
The firm also offers on-the-ground program delivery services to keep programs moving, with Avicado specialists serving as owner representatives, supporting site selection and feasibility, managing procurement services, and providing controls, schedule and document management.

Its team of more than 190 professionals will join Accenture Construct in the United States.

Shaw, CEO of Accenture Construct. “It’s our next move to give owners the full breadth of capabilities they need—proven industry platforms, people and process, and AI—and enabling us to take greater accountability for client outcomes.”

Price action for Accenture showed strength after two analysts raised price targets following the company's AI-focused growth strategy. TD Cowen’s Bryan C. Bergin lifted his target to $201 from $193, while Susquehanna’s James Friedman raised his to $230 from $210. The firm outlined a multi-year plan targeting revenue growth, margin expansion, and shareholder returns. Accenture expects mid-single-digit revenue growth in 2027 and 2028, with acceleration in 2029. Free cash flow and operating margin expansion remain key goals. The stock now appears to be testing new support and resistance levels.
TD Cowen analyst Bryan C. Bergin raised Accenture's price target from $193 to $201 while keeping a Hold rating. Susquehanna analyst James Friedman raised Accenture's price target from $210 to $230 while maintaining a Neutral rating. The increases followed Accenture's Investor Day on Wednesday. Accenture outlined a multi-year strategy focused on revenue growth, continued margin expansion, strong free cash flow and shareholder returns through dividends and share repurchases.
Accenture expects mid-single-digit revenue growth in local currency in fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2028. Accenture expects growth to accelerate to mid- to high-single-digit growth in fiscal 2029. Accenture targets annual operating margin expansion of 10 to 30 basis points throughout fiscal 2027 through fiscal 2029. Accenture expects a free cash flow-to-net income ratio of at least 1.1 times in fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2028. Accenture expects that ratio to rise to 1.2 to 1.3 times in fiscal 2029. Accenture also targets at least $9.5 billion in free cash flow in fiscal 2029.
Accenture plans to return cash to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases. Accenture targets a dividend payout ratio in the mid-40% range of prior-year net income in fiscal 2027. Bergin said Accenture presented a clear growth strategy as enterprise AI adoption expands. Bergin highlighted opportunities in capital projects, data and AI services, mid-market clients and operational technology cybersecurity. However, investors remain focused on whether Accenture can accelerate growth despite AI-driven efficiencies. Execution in fiscal 2027 will be crucial to validating Accenture's growth outlook. Accenture's multi-year growth framework draws on experience across more than 18,000 AI projects and an increase in Data and AI engagements worth more than $50 million. Bergin added that the fiscal 2027 through fiscal 2029 outlook depends on improving macroeconomic conditions and sustained mid-single-digit growth in Accenture's core business. Accenture's core business accounts for 94% of revenue. Ongoing modernization in enterprise resource planning, cloud, cybersecurity and data is expected to provide further growth opportunities.
Friedman said past technology shifts, including offshoring, cloud and digital adoption, reduced costs and replaced some IT services but also stimulated business-services demand, supporting Accenture's growth. Accenture, Dragos and SANS Institute Launch Foundation to Strengthen Cyber Defenses for Under-Resourced U.S. Utilities
Accenture, Dragos Inc. and the SANS Institute today announced a major initiative to help strengthen cyber defenses for under-resourced U.S. water, electric and natural gas utilities.
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 12:59 PM CDT 7 min read
Approximately $10 million in initial funding and services will support essential services relied on by more than 100 million Americans
Initiative will provide technology, deployment services and training at no cost to up to 500 under-resourced utilities
COLUMBUS, Ohio, October 20, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Accenture (NYSE: ACN), Dragos Inc. and the SANS Institute today announced a major initiative to help strengthen cyber defenses for under-resourced U.S. water, electric and natural gas utilities. These utilities provide essential services but often lack resources for adequate protection for their operational technology (OT) environments. The announcement comes amid a recent surge in cyberattacks targeting more than 100 U.S. water systems across over a dozen states.
In its first phase, the initiative will provide cybersecurity software, hardware, deployment services and SANS training free of charge to up to 500 under-resourced utilities. Accenture, Dragos and SANS are making an initial combined commitment of approximately $10 million in funding and services. In addition, Elastic is supporting the initiative through technology that allows for software delivery at scale by providing the primary log storage and query engine within the Dragos Platform.
Many of the tens of thousands of small utilities across the U.S., particularly those serving rural or underserved communities, face limited funding, workforce shortages and aging technology. This leaves the pumps, valves, substations and distribution networks that support essential services vulnerable to cyberattacks that can threaten public safety.
To address this gap, Accenture, Dragos and SANS are launching the Community Cyber Resilience Foundation to provide eligible utilities with OT cybersecurity technology, deployment support, hardware and training. The initiative builds on the Dragos Community Defense Program, which provides more than 100 utilities with free access to the Dragos Platform. The foundation was announced at a roundtable discussion focused on strengthening the cybersecurity of utilities in Ohio, hosted by American Electric Power (AEP) subsidiary Ohio Power Company, Accenture and Dragos.
"Our work with America's critical infrastructure operators has shown both the gravity of the cyber threats they face and a widening vulnerability gap—between large operators with the resources to invest in cybersecurity and smaller utilities that often lack those means," said Julie Sweet, chair and CEO, Accenture. "Together with Dragos and SANS, we will provide under-resourced utilities with the technology, expertise and training they need to better power and protect the communities they serve."
"Adversaries are aggressively targeting utilities, attacking the operational environments that provide life-sustaining services to millions of Americans. Yet many small operators lack the capacity to defend against these threats," said Robert M. Lee, Chairman, CEO, and Founder of Dragos. "The Community Cyber Resilience Foundation gives the utilities that need it most access to cybersecurity resources and training at no cost."
Eligible participants include U.S. based water, wastewater, electric and natural gas utilities with less than $100 million in annual revenue. More than 97% of utilities fall below this threshold, representing more than 50,000 organizations that may need support. Participants can expect:
Access to the Dragos Platform and services to help organizations know what's on their networks and how to address vulnerabilities and threats. Elasticsearch provides the underlying log storage and search capabilities that help Dragos deliver the platform at scale to participating utilities.
Accenture deployment services including expert configuration, integration and ongoing support.
SANS ICS/OT training to build and sustain in-house capabilities.
Hardware and infrastructure funding to purchase the equipment needed to deploy and run the Dragos Platform.
Peer community access connecting participants to a network of utilities sharing operational experience.
"The best security technology in the world won't protect a utility if its staff are not able to use it. The foundation puts training and skills in the hands of the people protecting the water, power, natural gas, and wastewater treatment systems that communities rely on," said James Lyne, CEO, SANS.
"Strong cybersecurity depends on many technologies working together. Elastic is committed to supporting Dragos in delivering its platform at scale, helping make advanced cybersecurity capabilities accessible to utilities that could not otherwise afford them," said Ashutosh Kulkarni, CEO, Elastic.
Utilities interested in participating can learn more at https://www.ccrfoundation.org/.
About the Community Cyber Resilience Foundation
The Community Cyber Resilience Foundation is a nonprofit launched by Accenture, Dragos, and the SANS Institute. It raises and provides the funding, hardware, deployment services, and training that small, under-resourced utilities in the U.S. need to secure their operational technology environments. Accenture reports before the open with five straight EPS beats behind it, so consensus of $3.18 is the low bar. The real tell is whether AI consulting demand is still offsetting cautious enterprise IT budgets.
Accenture reports fiscal fourth-quarter results before the opening bell on October 1, and five consecutive quarters of beating Wall Street's earnings-per-share estimate mean the market will treat anything merely in line with the $3.18 consensus as a disappointment.
The more consequential question sitting underneath that number is what management says about AI-driven consulting demand. Investors have been watching whether that business is strong enough to absorb the drag from corporations still guarding their broader IT budgets carefully, and the language in the outlook will carry as much weight as the headline figure.

WASHINGTON, October 19, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Accenture Federal Services, a subsidiary of Accenture (NYSE: ACN), and Google Public Sector today announced the deployment of Gemini launchpads, a new capability designed to help federal agencies move more quickly from agentic experimentation to mission execution at scale.
This initiative, which builds on the recent announcement of Accenture's Gemini Enterprise Business Group (part of the Accenture Google Business Group), provides federal agencies with a centralized hub of Forward Deployed Engineers (FDEs) to industrialize how they build, deploy, and scale enterprise agents. By embedding these specialized FDEs alongside agencies, the government can focus on delivering outcome-based, high-code agents built on Gemini, that integrate directly into core government systems of record and enable practitioners to execute complex workflows.
By activating a Gemini launchpad, agencies can centrally manage the agent–from securely connecting Gemini to mission datasets and prioritizing agent use cases to rapid deployment and workforce training. This provides leadership with a single view to track performance, measure mission impact, and drive even more value from their investment in Gemini.
"The real opportunity to scale value for our clients is deploying these purpose-built agents to transform work at the heart of government operations," said Ron Ash, CEO of Accenture Federal Services. "By embedding our Forward Deployed Engineers with agency teams, we're working side-by-side with our clients to help them define and rapidly solve their most critical challenges using agents to help deliver the advantage our clients need and the results they expect."
"Federal agencies stand at the threshold of the agentic era, where success is measured not merely by technology adopted, but by mission outcomes delivered," said Karen Dahut, CEO of Google Public Sector. "By pairing Gemini and secure cloud infrastructure with Accenture Federal Services' deep federal acumen, we are enabling agencies to build purpose-driven agents designed for the way they work. This collaboration further moves governments beyond incremental modernization—equipping public servants with intelligent capabilities to navigate complex systems, accelerate critical decisions, and deliver at the speed of mission."
Accelerating Mission Impact with Specialized Engineers and Pre-Built Agents
To meet federal demand and accelerate this mission, Accenture Federal Services is training an initial cohort of Google Cloud- skilled FDEs. This training would be part of Accenture's recently announced commitment to establish a 1,000-person FDE workforce Accenture Gemini Enterprise Business Group.
These FDEs will embed directly alongside agency teams and Accenture Federal's functional subject matter experts to bridge the gap between technology and mission. By combining advanced Google Cloud technical skills with deep federal domain expertise, these integrated teams will build Gemini agents that address real agency challenges and unlock tangible mission value.
To jumpstart agency adoption, Accenture Federal Services and Google Public Sector are developing a core set of pre-built agents across common mission-critical functions including HR, finance, and supply chain. These agents are purpose-built to streamline daily operations directly within Gemini. By handling complex workflows and data-gathering behind the scenes, these agents free federal employees to focus on decision-making and strategic mission execution.
"Executing this vision requires a combination of the right technology and mission experience," said Garrett Berntsen, Chief AI Officer, Accenture Federal Services. "Google Public Sector provides the industry-leading infrastructure and frontier models, while Accenture Federal brings the deep domain expertise and engineering talent needed to solve complex mission challenges. Together, we are putting Google's integrated tech stack to work to drive measurable outcomes for our customers."
Federal agencies can see these capabilities in action by engaging in collaborative, hands-on agent building workshops hosted jointly with Google Public Sector at The Forge in Washington, D.C. Recently launched within The Forge, The Prototyping Lab is a dedicated agentic prototyping space designed specifically to walk agency leaders through diverse, live agent experiences across various business and mission functions. During these interactive sessions, Accenture and Google Public Sector collaborate directly to identify the highest-impact agents for specific outcomes and outline a tactical roadmap to get started.

The initiative builds on the Dragos Community Defense Program, which provides more than 100 utilities with free access to the Dragos Platform. The foundation was announced at a roundtable discussion focused on strengthening the cybersecurity of utilities in Ohio, hosted by American Electric Power (AEP) subsidiary Ohio Power Company, Accenture and Dragos.
“Our work with America’s critical infrastructure operators has shown both the gravity of the cyber threats they face and a widening vulnerability gap—between large operators with the resources to invest in cybersecurity and smaller utilities that often lack those means,” said Julie Sweet, chair and CEO, Accenture. “Together with Dragos and SANS, we will provide under-resourced utilities with the technology, expertise and training they need to better power and protect the communities they serve.”
“Adversaries are aggressively targeting utilities, attacking the operational environments that provide life-sustaining services to millions of Americans. Yet many small operators lack the capacity to defend against these threats,” said Robert M. Lee, Chairman, CEO, and Founder of Dragos. “The Community Cyber Resilience Foundation gives the utilities that need it most access to cybersecurity resources and training at no cost.”
Who qualifies, how to apply Eligible participants include U.S. based water, wastewater, electric and natural gas utilities with less than $100 million in annual revenue. More than 97% of utilities fall below this threshold, representing more than 50,000 organizations that may need support. Participants can expect:
Access to the Dragos Platform and services to help organizations know what’s on their networks and how to address vulnerabilities and threats. Elasticsearch provides the underlying log storage and search capabilities that help Dragos deliver the platform at scale to participating utilities.
Accenture deployment services including expert configuration, integration and ongoing support.
SANS ICS/OT training to build and sustain in-house capabilities.
Hardware and infrastructurefunding to purchase the equipment needed to deploy and run the Dragos Platform.
Peer community access connecting participants to a network of utilities sharing operational experience.
“ The best security technology in the world won’t protect a utility if its staff are not able to use it. The foundation puts training and skills in the hands of the people protecting the water, power, natural gas, and wastewater treatment systems that communities rely on,” said James Lyne, CEO, SANS.
“Strong cybersecurity depends on many technologies working together. Elastic is committed to supporting Dragos in delivering its platform at scale, helping make advanced cybersecurity capabilities accessible to utilities that could not otherwise afford them,” said Ashutosh Kulkarni, CEO, Elastic.
Utilities interested in participating can learn more at https://www.ccrfoundation.org/.

Accenture sells AI transformation to thousands of clients while quietly telling its own employees they get a fraction of what some were already spending. The internal memo reveals a tension at the heart of every major consulting firm racing to…
Published October 16, 2026, 9:27am ET · 3 min read
A businessman engages in strategic planning amidst a backdrop of global AI innovation and financial data. The image underscores the intricate balance between technological advancement and sound personal finance in the rapidly evolving digital landscape. © MUNGKHOOD STUDIO / Shutterstock.com
An Accenture (NYSE:ACN | ACN Price Prediction) consultant building an AI solution for several clients said Claude Code usage ran between $500 and $1,000 a month. Starting October 1, the company will centrally fund $29 per person.
Accenture told many employees in an internal memo, reported on October 15, 2026, that it will pay only that fixed monthly amount toward Claude, the AI model built by privately held Anthropic. Anything above it must be charged to a project.
Accenture sells AI transformation to roughly 9,000 clients. Internally, it now limits spending on the same tools.
Shares rose 4.63% to $224.92 on October 15 during a broad software rally unrelated to the memo, yet they remain well below the 52-week high of $291.09.
What Accenture’s Claude Memo Actually Commits To
The memo, titled “Claude Enterprise Users: Important Updates to Licensing and Usage Costs,” states that “all costs are consumption-based.” Usage above the allowance goes to a Work Breakdown Structure (WBS), Accenture’s billing code for a project or team.
Heavy use remains possible, but it now needs a budget owner. Premium plans include $250 of weekly token usage, although many employees are not on Premium.
Access is conditional. The memo says, “Providing a WBS and obtaining a license does not guarantee indefinite or ongoing access to Claude,” and one employee lost access entirely.
Accenture did not publish the memo or say how many employees are affected. A spokesperson said, “Our approach today is to provide the right tool for the right work.”
Consumption Billing Shows What Coding AI Really Costs
The $29 cap targets a consumer subscription price point. Agentic coding tools, which carry out complex tasks on their own, consume far more tokens, the units AI models bill by.
One employee said usage topped $500 a month for months, and some spent as much as $1,000. Per-seat budgets are likely to fall short once work shifts to autonomous coding.
CEO Julie Sweet said on the October 1 earnings call that falling token costs will “enable companies to use AI in more places and at scale.” The memo suggests that prices likely have further to fall before agentic coding becomes cheap enough to fund on a per-seat basis.
Accenture earns its margin on labor across roughly 814,000 employees. Unlimited token spending on that base is a cost that grows without a matching revenue line.
Charging overruns to a WBS ties AI spending to client work. Fixed-price work is over 65% of bookings, so AI costs on those contracts land on Accenture unless they were priced in.
Management guided to a 15.9% to 16.1% operating margin for fiscal 2027, which leaves little room for unmanaged expense.
This is one policy, reported indirectly. Total spending, affected headcount, and whether other AI tools face similar limits remain unknown.
Accenture keeps expanding in AI, with nearly 110,000 AI and data professionals. Sweet also called the Anthropic relationship non-exclusive. For AI vendors, tight limits at the largest IT services firms could slow enterprise spending, although targeted use on proven work may last longer.
What Cost Discipline Means for Accenture’s Fiscal 2027 Outlook
The memo shows cost discipline that supports fiscal 2027 guidance for GAAP EPS of $14.39 to $14.81.
The gap from the 52-week high, with market value at $134.05 billion, reflects fears that AI will reduce IT services billing. A record 141 quarterly bookings of $100 million or more argue demand is holding.
The thesis fails if management says at the next earnings report that AI tool costs are pressuring margins, or if first-quarter revenue lands below the $18.95 billion low end of guidance.

Accenture, Dragos and SANS Institute Launch Foundation to Strengthen Cyber Defenses for Under-Resourced U.S. Utilities
Accenture, Dragos Inc. and the SANS Institute today announced a major initiative to help strengthen cyber defenses for under-resourced U.S. water, electric and natural gas utilities.
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 12:59 PM CDT 7 min read
Approximately $10 million in initial funding and services will support essential services relied on by more than 100 million Americans
Initiative will provide technology, deployment services and training at no cost to up to 500 under-resourced utilities
COLUMBUS, Ohio, October 20, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Accenture (NYSE: ACN), Dragos Inc. and the SANS Institute today announced a major initiative to help strengthen cyber defenses for under-resourced U.S. water, electric and natural gas utilities. These utilities provide essential services but often lack resources for adequate protection for their operational technology (OT) environments. The announcement comes amid a recent surge in cyberattacks targeting more than 100 U.S. water systems across over a dozen states.
In its first phase, the initiative will provide cybersecurity software, hardware, deployment services and SANS training free of charge to up to 500 under-resourced utilities. Accenture, Dragos and SANS are making an initial combined commitment of approximately $10 million in funding and services. In addition, Elastic is supporting the initiative through technology that allows for software delivery at scale by providing the primary log storage and query engine within the Dragos Platform.
Many of the tens of thousands of small utilities across the U.S., particularly those serving rural or underserved communities, face limited funding, workforce shortages and aging technology. This leaves the pumps, valves, substations and distribution networks that support essential services vulnerable to cyberattacks that can threaten public safety.
To address this gap, Accenture, Dragos and SANS are launching the Community Cyber Resilience Foundation to provide eligible utilities with OT cybersecurity technology, deployment support, hardware and training. The initiative builds on the Dragos Community Defense Program, which provides more than 100 utilities with free access to the Dragos Platform. The foundation was announced at a roundtable discussion focused on strengthening the cybersecurity of utilities in Ohio, hosted by American Electric Power (AEP) subsidiary Ohio Power Company, Accenture and Dragos.
"Our work with America's critical infrastructure operators has shown both the gravity of the cyber threats they face and a widening vulnerability gap—between large operators with the resources to invest in cybersecurity and smaller utilities that often lack those means," said Julie Sweet, chair and CEO, Accenture. "Together with Dragos and SANS, we will provide under-resourced utilities with the technology, expertise and training they need to better power and protect the communities they serve."
"Adversaries are aggressively targeting utilities, attacking the operational environments that provide life-sustaining services to millions of Americans. Yet many small operators lack the capacity to defend against these threats," said Robert M. Lee, Chairman, CEO, and Founder of Dragos. "The Community Cyber Resilience Foundation gives the utilities that need it most access to cybersecurity resources and training at no cost."
Eligible participants include U.S. based water, wastewater, electric and natural gas utilities with less than $100 million in annual revenue. More than 97% of utilities fall below this threshold, representing more than 50,000 organizations that may need support. Participants can expect:
Access to the Dragos Platform and services to help organizations know what's on their networks and how to address vulnerabilities and threats. Elasticsearch provides the underlying log storage and search capabilities that help Dragos deliver the platform at scale to participating utilities.
Accenture deployment services including expert configuration, integration and ongoing support.
SANS ICS/OT training to build and sustain in-house capabilities.
Hardware and infrastructure funding to purchase the equipment needed to deploy and run the Dragos Platform.
Peer community access connecting participants to a network of utilities sharing operational experience.
"The best security technology in the world won't protect a utility if its staff are not able to use it. The foundation puts training and skills in the hands of the people protecting the water, power, natural gas, and wastewater treatment systems that communities rely on," said James Lyne, CEO, SANS.
"Strong cybersecurity depends on many technologies working together. Elastic is committed to supporting Dragos in delivering its platform at scale, helping make advanced cybersecurity capabilities accessible to utilities that could not otherwise afford them," said Ashutosh Kulkarni, CEO, Elastic.
Utilities interested in participating can learn more at https://www.ccrfoundation.org/.
About the Community Cyber Resilience Foundation
The Community Cyber Resilience Foundation is a nonprofit launched by Accenture, Dragos, and the SANS Institute. It raises and provides the funding, hardware, deployment services, and training that small, under-resourced utilities in the U.S. need to secure their operational technology environments.
